experiment_design.technical_details: This experiment validates the hypothesis that inverse design algorithms using automatic differentiation (AD) can generate polypill geometries matching patient-specific drug-release kinetics. The core methodology adapts the PILL-CoDe framework [EV-Q015-d8c26e6621393a7b2da88789] to optimize geometry parameters (e.g., layer thickness, porosity distribution) against target release profiles. These target profiles are synthetically generated to represent inter-individual biological variability (e.g., varying metabolic rates and target plasma concentrations), addressing the knowledge gap regarding patient-specific constraints. The optimization loop minimizes the mean squared error (MSE) between simulated and target release curves using gradient-based optimizers enabled by AD. Feasible design spaces are constrained by physics-based requirements as described in heterogeneous constraint exploration methods [EV-Q015-2bf31247f850c054d922640e].

experiment_design.methods:
1. **Target Profile Generation**: Convert synthetic biological parameters into time-dependent drug release rate targets using compartmental pharmacokinetic models.
2. **Inverse Design Model**: Implement a differentiable physics simulator for drug diffusion/dissolution within polypill geometries. Use automatic differentiation to compute gradients of the loss function (difference between simulated and target release) with respect to geometric design variables.
3. **Optimization Loop**: Employ gradient descent (Adam optimizer) to iteratively update polypill geometry (layer thicknesses, internal channel structures) to minimize the deviation from the target profile.
4. **Constraint Handling**: Incorporate physical manufacturability constraints (minimum feature size, structural integrity) as penalty terms in the loss function, inspired by feasible design space exploration techniques [EV-Q015-2bf31247f850c054d922640e].

experiment_design.technical_details: This experiment validates the hypothesis that inverse design algorithms using automatic differentiation (AD) can generate polypill geometries matching patient-specific drug-release kinetics. The core methodology adapts the PILL-CoDe framework [EV-Q015-d8c26e6621393a7b2da88789] to optimize geometry parameters (e.g., layer thickness, porosity distribution) against target release profiles. These target profiles are synthetically generated to represent inter-individual biological variability (e.g., varying metabolic rates and target plasma concentrations), addressing the knowledge gap regarding patient-specific constraints. The optimization loop minimizes the mean squared error (MSE) between simulated and target release curves using gradient-based optimizers enabled by AD. Feasible design spaces are constrained by physics-based requirements as described in heterogeneous constraint exploration methods [EV-Q015-2bf31247f850c054d922640e].

experiment_design.methods:
1. **Target Profile Generation**: Convert synthetic biological parameters into time-dependent drug release rate targets using compartmental pharmacokinetic models.
2. **Inverse Design Model**: Implement a differentiable physics simulator for drug diffusion/dissolution within polypill geometries. Use automatic differentiation to compute gradients of the loss function (difference between simulated and target release) with respect to geometric design variables.
3. **Optimization Loop**: Employ gradient descent (Adam optimizer) to iteratively update polypill geometry (layer thicknesses, internal channel structures) to minimize the deviation from the target profile.
4. **Constraint Handling**: Incorporate physical manufacturability constraints (minimum feature size, structural integrity) as penalty terms in the loss function, inspired by feasible design space exploration techniques [EV-Q015-2bf31247f850c054d922640e].

experiments.validation_protocol: Split synthetic patient cases into training (for hyperparameter tuning of the optimizer) and test sets (N=50 distinct biological profiles). Evaluate the final designed geometries on the test set using the defined metrics. A successful validation requires >90% of test cases to achieve <10% deviation from target kinetics.
